gotcha-cs.cs.sh:
#!/bin/bash
# build one C# file the way the lessons do (the image's restored project), but keep
# the build's own output (timing lines) off the page unless the build fails
set -e
rm -rf /tmp/cs && cp -r /opt/templates/csharp /tmp/cs && cp "$1" /tmp/cs/Program.cs
cd /tmp/cs
dotnet build --no-restore -v q -nologo -clp:NoSummary > /tmp/cs-build.log 2>&1 || { cat /tmp/cs-build.log; exit 1; }
dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/Program.dll

gotcha.title: `let _ =` instead of `let _guard =`
gotcha.looks_fine: `_` is the usual name for a value you don't need: Go's `_ = x` throws a value away and Python's `_` is the convention for an unused one. So naming a guard `_` instead of `_guard` looks like a style choice.
gotcha.rust_sees: `let _ = counter.lock().unwrap();` does not bind the guard to any name, so it is dropped at the end of that statement and the lock is released at once. rustc has a lint for exactly this, `let_underscore_lock`, which is deny by default, so Rust refuses to compile it. A name like `_guard` keeps the guard alive until the end of the block.
gotcha.why: The lint exists for lock guards only. The same mistake with another guard is not caught: `let _ = span.enter();` compiles, and only the output tells you, because the span exits before the next log line (Try it yourself, task 3, shows that output). The other languages below show the scope version of the trap with a span-like object.

fixed.name: src/main.rs

go.says: `_ = Start(...)` throws the pointer away and nothing calls `End`. What closes a scope in Go is `defer`, which runs when the function returns, not when a value goes away.

enter request

kotlin.says: There is no `val _ = ...` form to show: in the Kotlin version in the image it does not compile without an experimental flag. Kotlin closes a resource with `use`, at the end of its block. A value you just create, like `Span("forgotten")` in the program shown, is never closed.
